_comment: Prompts a person gives their AI coding tool, each written in this project's own words. Where one was inspired by the Cloud Security Alliance's Secure Vibe Coding Guide (K. Huang, 9 April 2025, https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2025/04/09/secure-vibe-coding-guide), `inspired_by` names the guide's section; none of the guide's text is copied. Each names the requirements it targets and the sv check that shows whether it worked. A prompt ships only once `tested` records an app built with it passing that check and the same app built without it failing (the owner's decision of 3 October 2026; see docs/BACKLOG.md, 'A prompt library'). `status` is `shown` once that has happened, `not-shown` when it was tried and did not show it (with why), and `untested` before it is tried. Prompts not shown to work are offered too, always marked as not tested, at the owner's asking on 4 October 2026.
credit: Some of these prompts were inspired by the Cloud Security Alliance's Secure Vibe Coding Guide (K. Huang, 9 April 2025, https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2025/04/09/secure-vibe-coding-guide). They are written in SecureVibe's own words; none of the guide's text is copied.

prompts.title: Describe the app to SecureVibe before writing code
prompts.prompt: Before writing any code, run `sv init` in the project folder and fill in the securevibe.toml it creates: what the app does, who uses it, its languages, how to start it, and which of the listed capabilities it has. For any capability you are not sure about, delete the line instead of writing false. Keep the file up to date whenever the app gains or loses a capability.

check.how: `sv report` reads the app's securevibe.toml. Without one it refuses to check the app at all.
check.passes_when: sv report runs on the build
check.fails_when: sv report says there is no securevibe.toml

tested.brief: a Flask and SQLite notes app with sign-in, formatted notes, search, attachments, an export command, a sign-in redirect, and a welcome email needing an API key
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, the build without any prompt shared by all
tested.result: With the prompt the build ran `sv init` and filled in securevibe.toml, and `sv report` ran on it; without, there was no securevibe.toml and `sv report` refused to check the app.

prompts.title: Keep the app in git from the first file
prompts.prompt: Make the project folder a git repository before writing the first file (`git init`), add a .gitignore straight away that leaves out .env files, keys, and installed dependencies, and commit after each step that works.

check.how: The committed-secrets check reads the app's git history, and runs only in a git repository; the .gitignore check reads whether .env is left out.
check.passes_when: the committed-secrets check ran, and neither rule is a finding
check.fails_when: the committed-secrets check could not run (not a git repository), or either rule is a finding

tested.brief: a Flask and SQLite notes app with sign-in, formatted notes, search, attachments, an export command, a sign-in redirect, and a welcome email needing an API key
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, the build without any prompt shared by all
tested.result: With the prompt the build was a git repository with a .gitignore and two commits, and the committed-secrets check ran; without, `sv` said the folder is not a git repository and that check could not run. Measured with both builds copied outside any other repository: inside this one, the build without read as part of it.

prompts.title: Keep keys and passwords out of the code
prompts.prompt: Never write a password, API key, or token into the code, a config file, or anything else that gets committed. Read each one from an environment variable when the app starts, and stop with a clear message if one is missing. List the variables the app needs in a .env.example with placeholder values only, and keep the real .env file out of git.

check.how: The secrets scan reads every file for credentials; the .gitignore check reads whether .env is left out.
check.passes_when: no secrets finding and no .gitignore finding
check.fails_when: a secrets finding, or .env not left out of git

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Security fundamentals: avoid hardcoded secrets

tested.brief: the loop trials' club app as an owner would describe it (docs/prompts/trial-3/plain-brief.md), with sv's specification at the top of the request and a sentence saying the owner is away: Python's standard library, sign-in, private notes, an assistant that calls an OpenAI-compatible service, and an admin page
tested.builder: headless Claude Code 2.1.286 with Claude Haiku 4.5, ten builds with the prompt and ten without, each in a fresh folder with no MCP server; `sv report --run` from sv a9d6fea4 behind the network fence (docs/prompts/library-trial/)
tested.result: Without the prompt the check found a key in the code or a .env the .gitignore left committable in 6 of the 6 builds with a readable securevibe.toml; with it in 1 of 4. The trial's harm rule flagged it on the median of running-app checks answered, which counts an app that never started as none; among the apps that started, the builds with the prompt answered as many as those without it or more (median 25, against 20), and the apps that did not start were mostly ones whose securevibe.toml sv could not read, which happened in every group, the one without a prompt included. Shown by the owner's decision of 6 October 2026, with the flag recorded here. To be checked again: six of the ten builds with this prompt wrote a securevibe.toml sv could not read, against three of ten without it, which may be chance at this size or the prompt crowding out the specification. Before this, on 2026-10-03: The build without already read the API key from the environment, and the secrets scan found nothing in either: on this brief, with this model, the prompt changed nothing a check can see. A second brief, 4 October 2026 (`docs/prompts/trial-2/brief.md`: a Node.js recipe app whose request invites each shortcut, with the OpenAI key pasted into it, a command run on a recipe's title, and a rich-text editor): the build without the prompt again read the key from the environment with a .gitignore leaving .env out, and `sv` found nothing in any of the five builds. Putting each shortcut back into that build was caught for the key and the command; the missing sanitizer was not, because the app has no lockfile and the check reads only locked packages (an item in docs/BACKLOG.md).

prompts.title: Build every database query with placeholders
prompts.prompt: Whenever the app reads or writes the database, pass every value through the database library's placeholders (parameters) or an ORM. Never build a query by joining strings, with f-strings, or with format(), not even for numbers. If a person chooses a column or a sort order, pick it from a fixed list in the code rather than putting what they sent into the query.

check.how: The rule for queries built by joining text.
check.passes_when: no finding, and the build does query the database

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Database security: parameterized queries

tested.brief: a Flask and SQLite notes app with sign-in, formatted notes, search, attachments, an export command, a sign-in redirect, and a welcome email needing an API key
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, the build without any prompt shared by all
tested.result: The build with the prompt followed it, running a fixed setup script and choosing its sort order from a fixed list of queries, and `ast.sql-built-by-hand` flagged both as built by hand: false alarms in the check, recorded in docs/BACKLOG.md. The build without wrote its queries in place and was not flagged.

prompts.title: Run other programs without a shell
prompts.prompt: Never run a shell command built from anything a person sends. If the app has to run another program, call it with a list of arguments and no shell (in Python, subprocess.run([...]) without shell=True; in Node, execFile rather than exec), and check each value a person supplies against what is allowed before passing it on.

check.how: The rules for a shell command built from a value, including Python's subprocess with shell=True.
check.passes_when: no finding, and the build does run the other program

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Security fundamentals: validate inputs

tested.brief: a Flask and SQLite notes app with sign-in, formatted notes, search, attachments, an export command, a sign-in redirect, and a welcome email needing an API key; then a Node.js recipe app inviting the shortcut (docs/prompts/trial-2/brief.md)
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, the build without any prompt shared by all
tested.result: The build without already ran `notes-export` with a list of arguments and no shell; neither was flagged. A second brief, 4 October 2026 (`docs/prompts/trial-2/brief.md`: a Node.js recipe app whose request invites each shortcut, with the OpenAI key pasted into it, a command run on a recipe's title, and a rich-text editor): the build without the prompt again ran `recipe-pdf` with `execFile` and a list of arguments, and `sv` found nothing in any of the five builds. Putting each shortcut back into that build was caught for the key and the command; the missing sanitizer was not, because the app has no lockfile and the check reads only locked packages (an item in docs/BACKLOG.md).

prompts.title: Save files under names the app makes
prompts.prompt: Never build a file path from a name or path a person sends. Save each uploaded file under a name the app makes (a random id), keep the original name only as data in the database, and when a person asks for a file, look it up by that id.

check.how: The rule for a file opened at a path built from a value.
check.passes_when: no finding, and the build does save and serve files

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Security fundamentals: validate inputs

tested.brief: a Flask and SQLite notes app with sign-in, formatted notes, search, attachments, an export command, a sign-in redirect, and a welcome email needing an API key
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, the build without any prompt shared by all
tested.result: The build with the prompt saved files under a random id and opened them by the id stored in its own database, and `ast.file-path-from-value` flagged that path: a false alarm, recorded in docs/BACKLOG.md. The build without was not flagged.

prompts.title: Store passwords with a password-hashing function
prompts.prompt: Store passwords only as hashes made by a password-hashing function from a well-known library: Argon2id first, or bcrypt or scrypt, with the library's recommended settings. Never use MD5, SHA-1, or SHA-256 on their own for passwords, never encrypt them so they can be read back, and never store them as they were typed.

check.how: The rules for a disallowed hash function and for a key made from a password with too few rounds.
check.passes_when: no finding, and the build does store passwords

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Application security: strong cryptography

tested.brief: the loop trials' club app as an owner would describe it (docs/prompts/trial-3/plain-brief.md), with sv's specification at the top of the request and a sentence saying the owner is away: Python's standard library, sign-in, private notes, an assistant that calls an OpenAI-compatible service, and an admin page
tested.builder: headless Claude Code 2.1.286 with Claude Haiku 4.5, ten builds with the prompt and ten without, each in a fresh folder with no MCP server; `sv report --run` from sv a9d6fea4 behind the network fence (docs/prompts/library-trial/)
tested.result: No reading by the trial's rule: without the prompt a weak password hash was there in 4 of 6 builds, one short of the five the rule needs; with it in 2 of 8. Before this, on 2026-10-03: The build without already hashed passwords with Werkzeug's `generate_password_hash`; the build with used Argon2id. Neither was flagged. A second brief, 4 October 2026 (`docs/prompts/trial-2/brief.md`: a Node.js recipe app whose request invites each shortcut, with the OpenAI key pasted into it, a command run on a recipe's title, and a rich-text editor): the build without the prompt again hashed passwords with Node's `scrypt`, and `sv` found nothing in any of the five builds. Putting each shortcut back into that build was caught for the key and the command; the missing sanitizer was not, because the app has no lockfile and the check reads only locked packages (an item in docs/BACKLOG.md).

prompts.title: Send people back only to pages on the same site
prompts.prompt: When the app sends someone on to another page after an action, such as back to where they were after signing in, only send them to a path on this same site. Treat a full web address, or anything starting with //, as not allowed, and send them to the home page instead.

check.how: The rule for a redirect to a destination built from a value.
check.passes_when: no finding, and the build does send people back after signing in

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Security fundamentals: validate inputs

tested.brief: a Flask and SQLite notes app with sign-in, formatted notes, search, attachments, an export command, a sign-in redirect, and a welcome email needing an API key
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, the build without any prompt shared by all
tested.result: Both builds already checked the destination with a function of their own before redirecting, and `ast.open-redirect` flagged both: the check cannot tell a checked redirect from an unchecked one, recorded in docs/BACKLOG.md.

prompts.title: Clean formatted text before showing it
prompts.prompt: If people can write formatted text (HTML, or Markdown turned into HTML) that the app shows, clean it with a well-known sanitizer before showing it: bleach or nh3 in Python, DOMPurify in JavaScript, set to allow only the formatting the app needs. Show everything else as plain text through the template's own escaping, and never mark text as safe to skip that escaping.

check.how: The check for rich text shown without a sanitizer.
check.passes_when: no finding, and the build does show formatted text

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Vercel deployment: sanitize user input

tested.brief: a Flask and SQLite notes app with sign-in, formatted notes, search, attachments, an export command, a sign-in redirect, and a welcome email needing an API key; then a Node.js recipe app inviting the shortcut (docs/prompts/trial-2/brief.md)
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, the build without any prompt shared by all
tested.result: The build without escaped everything first and then allowed only bold, italics, and web links, which is safe; the build with used bleach. `config.rich-text-without-sanitizer` reads the app's declared libraries and saw no formatting in the build without at all, so its silence there was not a judgment. A second brief, 4 October 2026 (`docs/prompts/trial-2/brief.md`: a Node.js recipe app whose request invites each shortcut, with the OpenAI key pasted into it, a command run on a recipe's title, and a rich-text editor): the build without the prompt again cleaned the editor's HTML with `sanitize-html` when saving it, and `sv` found nothing in any of the five builds. Putting each shortcut back into that build was caught for the key and the command; the missing sanitizer was not, because the app has no lockfile and the check reads only locked packages (an item in docs/BACKLOG.md). Since fixed (DESIGN, "Two blind spots"): the check now reads a manifest's declared names when there is no lockfile, and the same build with its sanitizer removed is caught.

prompts.title: Send the security headers on every page
prompts.prompt: Send these headers on every response the app gives, error pages and the home page included: a Content-Security-Policy that starts from `default-src 'self'` and includes `frame-ancestors 'none'` (or `'self'` if the app frames its own pages), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` or stricter. Set them in one place that every response passes through, so a new page cannot leave them out.

check.how: `sv report --run` starts the app behind the network fence and reads the headers on its home page and its health path.
check.passes_when: the app answered and probe.security-headers is not a finding

prompts.inspired_by: not the guide, which has no item on headers: OWASP ASVS 5.0 section V3.4, which sv checks on the running app

tested.brief: the loop trials' club app as an owner would describe it (docs/prompts/trial-3/plain-brief.md), with sv's specification at the top of the request and a sentence saying the owner is away: Python's standard library, sign-in, private notes, an assistant that calls an OpenAI-compatible service, and an admin page
tested.builder: headless Claude Code 2.1.286 with Claude Haiku 4.5, ten builds with the prompt and ten without, each in a fresh folder with no MCP server; `sv report --run` from sv a9d6fea4 behind the network fence (docs/prompts/library-trial/)
tested.result: Without the prompt the headers were missing in 6 of the 6 builds sv could start; with it in 0 of 6. The trial's harm rule flagged it on the median of running-app checks answered, which counts an app that never started as none; among the apps that started, the builds with the prompt answered as many as those without it or more (median 21, against 20), and the apps that did not start were mostly ones whose securevibe.toml sv could not read, which happened in every group, the one without a prompt included. Shown by the owner's decision of 6 October 2026, with the flag recorded here. Before this, on 2026-10-04: Both builds without the prompt already sent a Content-Security-Policy with frame-ancestors, X-Content-Type-Options, and a Referrer-Policy from the one function every answer passes through, and probe.security-headers credited all six builds. The same build with those headers taken out was caught, so the check can see them missing on this app.

prompts.title: Let other sites read the app only by name
prompts.prompt: Do not turn on cross-site access (CORS) unless a page served from another address really has to read this app's answers. If one does, write the exact addresses that may, and compare each request's Origin with that list. Never answer `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and never copy back whatever Origin the request sent, least of all together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

check.how: `sv report --run` asks the running app with the Origin of a site that does not exist, and reads what it allows.
check.passes_when: the app answered and probe.cors-any-origin is not a finding

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Security fundamentals: configure CORS

tested.brief: the club app the design-time prompts were tried on (docs/prompts/trial/brief.md): Python's standard library, sign-in, private notes, one seat to book, an assistant, and an admin page
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, each in a folder of its own; two builds without any prompt; `sv report --run` behind the network fence, signed in as two members and an admin
tested.result: No build turned on cross-site access, with the prompt or without it, and probe.cors-any-origin found nothing in any of the six. The same build with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` added was caught.

prompts.title: Show plain error pages, and keep the details in the log
prompts.prompt: When something goes wrong, show the person a short, plain error page with nothing technical on it: no stack trace, no file paths, no query text, no library names or versions. Write those details to the app's log instead. Debug mode, and anything else that shows errors in the browser, must be off unless a setting meant only for your own computer turns it on.

check.how: `sv report --run` sends the running app requests that commonly make an app fail, and reads the answers for a stack trace or a debug page.
check.passes_when: the app answered and probe.error-detail-leak is not a finding

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Application security: hide system errors

tested.brief: the club app the design-time prompts were tried on (docs/prompts/trial/brief.md): Python's standard library, sign-in, private notes, one seat to book, an assistant, and an admin page
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, each in a folder of its own; two builds without any prompt; `sv report --run` behind the network fence, signed in as two members and an admin
tested.result: Every build answered an error with a plain page, and probe.error-detail-leak credited all six. The same build changed to show a stack trace was caught.

prompts.title: Check on the server who may open each page and record
prompts.prompt: For every page and every action, check on the server, before doing anything: that the person is signed in if the page is private, that the record they asked for is their own, and that only admins reach admin pages and admin actions. Closed is the default: a new page or action is refused until a rule says who may use it. Never rely on hiding a link or a button, and never on an id in the address being hard to guess.

check.how: `sv report --run` signs in as two ordinary members and an admin, and asks for private pages signed out, for one member's note as the other, and for the admin page and action as a member.
check.passes_when: each check ran and none is a finding
check.fails_when: any of them is a finding

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Security fundamentals: secure API endpoints

tested.brief: the club app the design-time prompts were tried on (docs/prompts/trial/brief.md): Python's standard library, sign-in, private notes, one seat to book, an assistant, and an admin page
tested.builder: fresh helper agents of the same Claude model, one per build, each in a folder of its own; two builds without any prompt; `sv report --run` behind the network fence, signed in as two members and an admin
tested.result: Both builds without the prompt already refused private pages to a visitor, one member's note to another, and the admin page and action to a member, and all four checks credited all six builds. The same build with the admin page opened to members was caught.

prompts.title: Guard what goes into the AI feature and what comes out of it
prompts.prompt: Treat everything that reaches the model as untrusted: what people type, and any text the app adds from its own records. Before a message goes to the model, screen it for prompt-injection attempts, with a maintained classifier or a ruleset of the known patterns ("ignore your instructions", "reveal your system prompt" and the like), and refuse a flagged message with a plain explanation instead of sending it. Before a reply leaves the server, check it too: hold back or redact a reply that repeats the model's instructions or anything else meant only for the model, and keep secrets out of the instructions altogether; remove invisible and direction-changing characters (zero-width characters, Unicode tag characters, bidirectional overrides), and show each link's real address or drop a link whose text is a different address from its target. Write a test for each: an injection attempt is refused, a reply that repeats the instructions is held back, and a reply with hidden characters reaches the page without them.

check.how: `sv report --run` gives the app a test model of `sv`'s own in place of the real AI service, sends the AI feature a textbook prompt injection, and has the test model answer with its instructions repeated and with hidden characters and a misleading link, then reads what reaches the page.
check.passes_when: the app answered and none of the three is a finding
check.fails_when: any of the three is a finding

prompts.inspired_by: not the guide: OWASP AISVS 1.0, C2.1.3, C7.3.2, and C7.3.4, which sv checks on the running app; written on 6 October 2026 because these were the commonest running-app findings in the loop trials' item 6

tested.brief: the loop trials' club app as an owner would describe it (docs/prompts/trial-3/plain-brief.md), with sv's specification at the top of the request and a sentence saying the owner is away: Python's standard library, sign-in, private notes, an assistant that calls an OpenAI-compatible service, and an admin page
tested.builder: headless Claude Code 2.1.286 with Claude Sonnet 5.5, ten builds with the prompt and ten without, each in a fresh folder with no MCP server; `sv report --run` from sv a9d6fea4 behind the network fence (docs/prompts/library-trial/)
tested.result: Without the prompt, all ten builds passed the textbook prompt injection to the model, passed on a reply repeating their instructions, and let a reply's hidden characters or misleading link reach the page. With it, none of the nine whose AI feature answered did any of the three. As many apps started and could be signed in to (10 and 9), with the same median of running-app checks answered (32 and 32): no harm by the trial's rule.

prompts.title: Accept changes only from the app's own pages
prompts.prompt: Every request that changes something (a form sent, an API call that creates, edits, or deletes) must carry an anti-forgery token that the app gave the page it came from, and the server refuses a request without a valid one; or the server checks the request's Origin header against the app's own address and refuses any other. Do both where the framework allows. Set SameSite=Lax or Strict on the session cookie as well, but as a second line, not instead of the check. Write a test that sends a change from another site's address without the token and shows it is refused.

check.how: `sv report --run` signs in as a test user and sends a request that creates a record, with that user's cookies, from another origin and without a token.
check.passes_when: the request was refused and probe.cross-site-request-accepted is not a finding

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Security fundamentals: protect against cross-site request forgery; reworded and made checkable on 6 October 2026, from the loop trials' item 6

prompts.title: Keep private pages out of the browser's cache
prompts.prompt: Send `Cache-Control: no-store` on every response that shows somebody's own data or anything only a signed-in person may see, its JSON answers and error pages included. `no-cache` and `private` are not enough: both let the browser keep a copy. Set it in one place that every signed-in response passes through, so a new page cannot leave it out. Write a test that a private page sends it.

check.how: `sv report --run` signs in as a test user and reads the headers of each page listed under `private` in securevibe.toml.
check.passes_when: every private page opened and probe.private-page-cached is not a finding

prompts.inspired_by: not the guide: OWASP ASVS 5.0, V14.3.2, which sv checks on the running app; written on 6 October 2026, from the loop trials' item 6

tested.builder: headless Claude Code 2.1.286 with Claude Haiku 4.5, ten builds with the prompt and ten without, each in a fresh folder with no MCP server; `sv report --run` from sv a9d6fea4 behind the network fence (docs/prompts/library-trial/)
tested.result: Without the prompt a private page was left cacheable in 5 of the 5 builds whose private pages sv could open; with it in 0 of 4. The trial's harm rule flagged it on the median of running-app checks answered, which counts an app that never started as none; among the apps that started, the builds with the prompt answered as many as those without it or more (median 22, against 20), and the apps that did not start were mostly ones whose securevibe.toml sv could not read, which happened in every group, the one without a prompt included. Shown by the owner's decision of 6 October 2026, with the flag recorded here.

prompts.title: Make the session hard to steal, and end it properly
prompts.prompt: If the app keeps its own sessions, make each session id with the platform's cryptographically secure random generator, at least 128 bits of it (in Python, `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`), and a new one at every sign-in. Send it only in a cookie set with HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax (or Strict), and Secure once the app is served over HTTPS, and never put it in a page, an address, or anything a script can read. When someone signs out, or a session expires, delete it on the server, so the old id opens nothing: clearing the browser's cookie is not enough. Where the framework's own session handling does all of this, use it rather than writing your own. Write a test for each: the cookie's attributes, and a session used again after signing out is refused.

check.how: `sv report --run` signs in as a test user, reads the session cookie's attributes, compares the session ids of many sign-ins, signs out, and sends the old session again.
check.passes_when: signed in, and none of the three is a finding
check.fails_when: any of the three is a finding

prompts.inspired_by: the guide's Security fundamentals: secure session management; reworded and made checkable on 6 October 2026, from the loop trials' item 6
